transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Um, it's nice to meet you too. So, I guess what brings me in is... well, I'm having a really, really hard time at work lately. I work at a meat processing plant right now—which, I know, isn't exactly what people expect when I tell them I just finished my bachelor's degree, but the money is decent while I figure things out. But the thing is, it's a very strict environment. There are all these protocols, and I just... I keep starting things and not finishing them. 

Like, I'll start the sanitation steps—and those are a huge deal, obviously, because it's meat processing and you absolutely cannot mess around with cross-contamination—or I'll sit down to do the batch logs or the end-of-line paperwork. I'll get the clipboard, I'll go through the first few sections, and then somehow I just... I leave out the last parts. 

And the worst part is, I know my job depends on finishing them correctly. Like, I am fully aware of how high the stakes are. The supervisors check everything, and if a batch log is missing the final temperature check or the sign-off at the very end, it can hold up the whole line. I tell myself every single morning, "You are going to finish the whole form today," and I start off fine, but then my brain just sort of... skips the end. I'll just walk away thinking I did it, or I get derailed right before the final step. My manager actually pulled me aside recently and was holding up my clipboard like, "Why is this bottom section blank again?" and I literally didn't have a good answer for him. I just felt so incredibly stupid. I don't understand why I can't just follow through to the end of a simple piece of paper when I know my job is on the line. I'm just terrified I'm going to get fired over this, and I don't know how to fix it.
Looking back at your time in elementary or middle school, did you experience these same kinds of struggles with finishing your assignments or staying on task?

Oh, yeah. Wow, yeah. It's funny you ask about elementary school because, well, my mom actually still has all my old report cards. She’s one of those people who saves absolutely everything, you know? Like, every drawing, every spelling test, every single report card in these big plastic bins in the basement. And a few months ago, when I first started realizing how bad things were getting at the plant, I actually went down there and dug through them because I was trying to figure out if I've always been like this or if I'm just losing my mind now. 

And, um, I found the ones from fourth grade—Mrs. Gable's class, I still remember her, she had this really loud laugh and wore these bright floral dresses—and right there in the comments section, it was like reading about myself right now. She wrote that I was "bright" and "capable," which is what they always say, right? But then she wrote that I needed constant, and I mean *constant*, reminders to finish my classwork. And my homework, too. I would do the homework, I swear I would do it, sitting at the kitchen table for hours, but then I just... wouldn't turn it in. It would just sit in my folder, or I'd forget to put my name on it, or I'd do the first page and completely forget there was a back side. 

I remember sitting in class, and I understood the lessons. Like, if she asked a question about the reading, I knew the answer. I wasn't confused by the material at all. But when she would give instructions for what to do next, it was like my brain would just check out after the first step. I'd miss whole chunks of what we were supposed to do unless she was literally standing right next to my desk, tapping on my paper. If she walked away to help someone else, I’d just drift off or stare at my pencil or start reading ahead in the book, and then suddenly everyone else was handing in their finished worksheets and I was still on question two. It was so frustrating because I knew I wasn't stupid, but I just couldn't seem to do the things everyone else was doing so easily. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, which I guess is why I'm so scared that I'm never going to outgrow it.

Aside from the trouble with finishing tasks, would you say you have always struggled with feeling physically restless, like you need to be constantly moving or have trouble sitting still for long periods?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think so? When I think about being restless, I picture those kids who were always bouncing off the walls, you know? Like the ones who would literally get up and run around the classroom or who couldn't stay in their chairs during an assembly. And that was never really me. 

I actually kind of liked sitting still, especially if I had a book or something I was actually interested in. Like, I could sit on the couch at home for hours just reading, completely zoned out. My mom used to joke that a bomb could go off and I wouldn't move, as long as I was reading one of my fantasy novels. So it wasn't a physical need to move around. I mean, sure, maybe I'd twirl my hair or doodle in the margins of my notebooks—oh, my notebooks were completely covered in doodles, like vines and stars and little geometric shapes all down the sides of the paper—but I wasn't, like, jumping out of my seat. 

Even now at the plant, we have to stand in one place on the line for long stretches, and the standing still part isn't what bothers me. It's the mental part. It's like my brain is the thing that's restless, if that makes sense? Like my thoughts are constantly ping-ponging all over the place, but my body is totally fine just staying put. I don't feel that physical itch to get up and pace or anything like that. I just... I just drift away mentally while my body stays right where it's supposed to be. So, yeah, I wouldn't say I'm physically restless at all, really. Just... mentally somewhere else.
In your daily life, how often do you find yourself losing or misplacing things that you need to complete your tasks, like your keys, your wallet, or your work equipment?

Oh my gosh, all the time. It is actually ridiculous how often it happens. Like, you mentioned work equipment, and that is exactly it—that is the absolute bane of my existence right now. On the floor at the plant, I am constantly, and I mean *constantly*, losing things I need just to do my basic job. 

My cut glove—which is this heavy metal mesh thing you absolutely have to wear so you don't slice your fingers off—my dry-erase marker for the logs, my employee badge, my safety glasses... I will lose them multiple times a shift. And the craziest part is, I’ll swear I just had them in my hand. Like, I can literally feel the phantom weight of the marker in my fingers, and I’ll go to write something on the board, and it’s just... not there. It’s like these things just vanish into thin air the exact second I stop actively staring at them. 

And then, of course, I have to spend ten minutes retracing my steps, just walking back and forth looking like a total idiot. I'll be patting down my smock pockets over and over, checking the break room, checking the hand-washing station, looking under the stainless steel tables... And ten minutes might not sound like a huge deal to most people, but on a meat processing line, ten minutes is an absolute eternity. Everything is timed to the second. People get so annoyed with me because you literally cannot be on the floor without your safety glasses or your cut glove. It's a massive safety violation. 

So I'm just running around in a total panic, digging through my locker, asking my coworkers if they've seen my badge, and they're all just staring at me like, "Really? Again?" It's so exhausting. It happens with my keys and my wallet at home, too, like you said, but the work stuff is what really terrifies me because it’s so public, you know? Everyone sees me wandering around looking for the exact same pair of safety glasses I was wearing five minutes ago, and I just don't know how to explain to them that my brain just deleted the memory of where I put them down.

When you are in a group setting, such as a conversation with friends or waiting in a queue, do you often find yourself blurting out answers before someone has finished speaking or struggling significantly with waiting your turn?

Oh, no, definitely not. Actually, it's usually the complete opposite for me. I'm the one who never speaks up in time. Like, if I'm hanging out with my friends from college—we still try to get together on weekends sometimes, usually just at someone's apartment because going out is so expensive right now—they'll be talking and debating something, and by the time I've actually processed what they said and formulated a response in my head, the conversation has completely moved on to a totally different topic. So I end up just sitting there quietly most of the time. I definitely don't interrupt people or blurt things out. I'm honestly too busy just trying to keep track of the conversation, which takes up all my mental energy anyway. 

And as for waiting my turn, like waiting in a line at the grocery store or at the cafeteria at the plant... honestly, I don't mind waiting at all. Like I was saying before about not being physically restless, waiting in a line is just another excuse for me to zone out. I'll just stand there, staring at the back of the person's head in front of me, completely lost in my own little world. I'll be thinking about a book I'm reading or trying to remember if I left my work boots near the heater at home so they'd dry out, and I'll just completely detach from where I am. 

Sometimes people actually have to tap me on the shoulder to tell me the line moved or the cashier is ready, because I'm just so spaced out. I'm never the one tapping my foot or huffing and puffing because things are taking too long. If anything, I'm perfectly content just existing in my own head while the world happens around me. So, no, blurting things out or getting impatient in lines... that really doesn't sound like me at all. I'm much more of the, um, the silent observer who completely forgets she's supposed to be participating.
